author: Jim Lowe Staff Writer
title: 'A Room in the Castle': Women of 'Hamlet' find themselves in taut thriller | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
‘Hamlet,” of course, is Shakespeare’s tragic tale of the Prince of Denmark seeking revenge for the murder of his father by his uncle Claudius, who has usurped the throne and married Hamlet’s mother Gertrude. The Prince feigns madness to protect himself while he makes plans, but he also rejects his betrothed Ophelia, breaking her heart.
This, one of the most powerful plays in the English language, explores the actions and deep emotions of the worst of ambitious men. But what of the women they trample upon to achieve their power?
Lauren Gunderson imagines “Hamlet” from the point of view the of the only two women in Shakespeare’s tragedy in her new play, “A Room in the Castle.” Gertrude, Ophelia and her handmaid Anna navigate the dangerous maze that is the court of Denmark in order to avoid the inevitable fate of all Shakespeare heroines — death!
“This play dances and duels with ‘Hamlet,’ foregrounding the women in the play and re-imagining them with agency, vitality, and radical hearts eager for a new ending,” says Gunderson.
Middlebury Acting Company will present Gunderson’s “A Room in the Castle,” directed by Margo Whitcomb, March 5-15 at Town Hall Theater in Middlebury.
“For such an iconic character, Shakespeare’s Ophelia is obscured in mystery,” says Mads Middleton, who is playing Ophelia. “We know very little about her canonically, and there are many gaps of knowledge to consider when you investigate Ophelia. Gunderson offers some clarity through her play, but there are still many questions to solve. I enjoy that kind of inquisitive relationship with a character.”
Joining Middleton from New York is Jena Necrason, a Vermont professional actor, as Gertrude.
This “is a rare opportunity to see a (very) new play, with a fully female artistic team, during a time in our lives when we must continue to lift up the voices of women, both ours today and the voices from our collective past,” she said.
And Laura Roald, another Vermont professional, is the handmaid Anna.
“I love the intrigue between the characters fighting to overcome the tide of tragedy in ‘Hamlet’,” she said. “The perspective of the women in the castle is sharp, funny and full of hope and dread.”
Gunderson was recognized by American Theatre magazine as the most produced American playwright. And, while many of her plays come across simplistic and pedantic, “A Room in the Castle” enjoys Shakespeare’s complexity in a genuine thriller.
“Gunderson is both prolific and she lifts up the voices of women throughout history,” says Whitcomb. “But her first love and the place that she most succeeds, in my opinion, is in this sort of Shakespeare and Shakespeare adjacent. It’s a great passion of hers.
“And I think that we feel that in this play,” Whitcomb said. “Certainly in my production, you’ll feel that there’s a sort of real passionate exhilaration about liberating these characters from the confines of the canonical ‘Hamlet’.”
The structure of Gunderson’s play has the three women together, as well as answering the unseen men in Shakespeare’s script.
“It keeps bouncing back and forth,” Whitcomb says. “It’s really sort of in conversation with the original ‘Hamlet.’ It’s really a new play, the new imagining of an old play, but also a wholly original play in conversation with the canonical ‘Hamlet’.”
Gunderson identifies the “Hamlet” scenes by where they fall in the play, “Act 5 Scene 2 of Hamlet,” for example.
“I’ve acted in ‘Hamlet’ twice and directed it and taught it taught it endlessly, I know it like the back of my hand, but that that doesn’t even mean anything to me,” Whitcomb says. “So instead of naming the scene with what feels to me like a little bit of an insider’s conceit, each of the projections very succinctly describes what’s happening rather than where it falls.”
How is Whitcomb making all this work?
“In the same way that Gunderson is filling in the blanks of ‘Hamlet’ in this play, I’m sort of filling in the blanks of ‘A Room in the Castle’,” she said.
Middlebury Acting Company has created an extensive and ambitious soundscape that involves music from a variety of genres and employs special effects.
“A kind of sonic representation of Hamlet in those scenes where a woman is talking to him but he’s not present,” Whitcomb.
This is only the third production of “A Room in the Castle.”
“Cincinnati Shakespeare actually commissioned the work. The director chose to completely modernize the — and I’m not doing that at all,” Whitcomb said. “What we’re playing with is that it’s a play that looks like it was then, in an imaginative landscape, and it becomes a play about now.
“To build that bridge from a kind of imagined classical period to today feels like a really interesting journey that I want to unfold gradually.”
As it’s early in the play’s history, Whitcomb feels free to tinker a bit to make it more effective with the audience she knows.
“I do think that one of the successes of the play, and I hope that I’ve amplified that, is that it’s basically a really sharp, funny and furious indictment of being silenced and invisible throughout history for women. Then and now.”
